references.text: Laying hands on the head of the sacrifice is a central ritual that symbolizes identification with the offering and the transfer of sin.
The elders of the congregation lay their hands on the head of the sin offering, the same ritual performed here by the Levites.
Aaron lays his hands on the scapegoat and confesses the sins of the people, a parallel laying-on-of-hands ritual.
At the consecration of priests, they lay their hands on the head of the bull before it is offered as a sin offering.
The burnt offering (עֹלָה) is mentioned here with the laying on of hands to make atonement.
The sin offering (חַטָּאת) is described as making atonement for sin, serving the same function as in this verse.
The combination of a sin offering and a burnt offering for atonement is an established pattern in the laws concerning sacrifices.
Earlier in the same chapter, the two bulls to be used for the sin offering and the burnt offering are mentioned.
It explains the theological basis of atonement (כַּפֵּר): the blood makes atonement for the soul.
The New Testament explains that almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.
